newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish budget foreign financing too costly - c.bank.
newsitem.headline: Polish budget foreign financing too costly - c.bank.

text.p: Poland's central bank is ready to to cut banks' mandatory reserves to help finance an increased budget deficit if the government agrees to give up its plans to seek additional financing abroad, the bank's deputy head said.
Witold Kozinski told Reuters in an interview on Monday that the bank believed foreign borrowing would prove more costly than additional financing in the domestic banking system.

"This can be treated as an offer that if the ministry gives up plans to finance the increased deficit abroad, we are ready to lower the mandatory reserves and thus increase banking liquidity which could be used for deficit financing," he said.

The finance ministry on Friday amended the 1997 budget draft, widening the deficit by 900 million zlotys to 12.2 billion or 2.8 percent of gross domestic product from the earlier planned 2.6 percent to accomodate lower income taxes.
Kozinski said foreign borrowing, regardless of the instrument used, would mean that interest paid would leave Poland rather than stay in the domestic banking system.

On the other hand lower mandatory reserves -- now at 17 percent for zloty call deposits, nine percent for zloty term deposits and two percent for foreign deposits -- would cut banks' costs, boost profits and consequently budget tax revenues.
The central bank has earlier criticised the original budget draft for radically increasing the share of domestic banks in the deficit financing to 6.7 billion from this year's 3.7 billion.
The bank warned that increased borrowing needs would translate into higher market interest rates.
But Finance Minister Grzegorz Kolodko pledged to limit deficit financing in the banking system by borrowing abroad or boosting privatisation revenues.

"I am surprised that in a situation when obligatory reserves are still at a relatively high level and represent a potential reservoir of liquidity one is using foreign borrowing to supplement deficit financing," Kozinski said.
The NBP earlier said that a bigger deficit could delay its plans to continue to gradually reduce the obligatory reserves for zloty deposits, for inflationary reasons.

Banks have been long lobbying for a cut in the reserves saying their current level was making money too costly and was putting them at a disadvantage to foreign competition, which had access to much cheaper funds.
